pr_title: Add out-of-order sample support to the TSDB
pr_body:
Closes https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/8535

This implementation is based on this design doc:
https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Kppm7qL9C-BJB1j6yb6-9ObG3AbdZnFUBYPNNWwDBYM/edit?usp=sharing

This commit adds support to accept out-of-order ("OOO") sample into the TSDB
up to a configurable time allowance. If OOO is enabled, overlapping queries
are automatically enabled.
pr_comments: Having some trouble making windows tests pass, will focus on this soon. Need to address other work first.
This is now ready for review :tada:  cc @codesome @bwplotka (I'm quoting you since you are both the tsdb maintainers)

Amazing! Planning to take a deep look tomorrow, great job 💪🏽 

What was that tricky bug that you managed to find @jesusvazquez  ? (curious - I love good debugging stories 🎉 )

@bwplotka it was this commit https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/11075/commits/faa90015d843f58d83e4518ad91d6d026840b662. It was mostly amplified with the distributed querying nature of Mimir and might not affect Prometheus. We have a cache for matcher->postings in mimir-prometheus for each block. The LabelValue call on the TSDB were checking the time ranges of the in-order head when asked for the out-of-order Head, which made it to return wrong results. And since OOO and in-order head share the index, and that postings cache, this wrong labels values made it to cache wrong postings for matchers (the label values result was used to query for samples). This resulted in wrong series being returned for a query 🙈 (for example, foo!=bar will give a series that has foo=bar)

Last few commits are also bug fixes. https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/11075/commits/710770e8a7dbad19903dd6b59fb8c53a435d70ff fixes a panic. https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/11075/commits/8daef745a03da4024523d26e8e28109e3df29f6b fixes a case where the disk was growing till it became full. (these were not tricky to identify)

:wave: @bwplotka glad you're going to have some time to review!

> What was that tricky bug that you managed to find @jesusvazquez ?

@codesome and I have been focused in finding two bugs :joy: 

**Bug 1** in Windows tests: It was a small thing, I believe Windows batches writes so when writing samples to the head chunk and then to memory mapped files we had to manually flush the files so the unit test expectations matched the ones we had on Linux. 

**Bug 2** on out of order queries that was fixed in this commit https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/11075/commits/faa90015d843f58d83e4518ad91d6d026840b662 We were after this for +2 weeks thats why the PR got delayed a bit. 

The story:

While designing the OOOHeadIndexReader we noticed most of the implementations could be shared with headIndexReader, thats why the OOOHeadIndexReader struct embeds a pointer to *headIndexReader and only overrides the Series() method.

Everything was looking good and all the tests we wrote were passing but we made the mistake of always querying the interval [math.MinInt, match.MaxInt] so the query interval was always the biggest it could be. However in real life that's not the real scenario, queries are usually for the last 5m, 30m, 1h, 1d, .... and this was leading to some gaps in the query results. This was happening in some production instances :scream: so this became our top priority.

After going through the code many many **many** times we realized that we were probably failing in the LabelValues method. We were reading the out of order head but comparing to the head mint and maxt not the head minooot and maxooot :scream: https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/b72fa96ca7902ea89f0481d06b13ba28d589e2e4/tsdb/head_read.go#L77-L79 The "shortcut" we made of leveraging on all the methods of headIndexReader was biting us. And that's why the solution present in the commit above overrides the method to have a proper condition checking.

The fix was actually just a few lines of code and a unit test to make sure this doesn't happen again but the amount of time spent ti find it out was huge :smile:

Really excited to see forward movement on this!
Also willing to help out if we can -- this has been a pretty annoying issue for our Prometheus deployments on GKE.

I was wondering, wouldn't it be easier and less complex to log to regular WAL after commit (some new committed_sample type) and implement cleanup to account for out-of-order samples, instead of the special and optional WBL? I lack context regarding implementation, so could be wrong here. This can be iterated on later as well! 🙂

> I was wondering, wouldn't it be easier and less complex to log to regular WAL after commit (some new committed_sample type) and implement cleanup to account for out-of-order samples, instead of the special and optional WBL? I lack context regarding implementation, so could be wrong here. This can be iterated on later as well! 🙂

We considered that in the beginning, but the problem comes when we are cleaning up the WAL. It is trivial to tell which samples to keep and which to throw away when we are cleaning up the WAL for the in-order data, we just need to know the min timestamp of the Head block (this is during the [checkpointing](http://ganeshvernekar.com/blog/prometheus-tsdb-wal-and-checkpoint#checkpointing) process). But we cannot tell if a OOO sample needs to be kept around or if it has been already compacted by looking at the timestamp. So we decided to keep it separate so that their cleanup gets simpler and less hacky. Do you think we might be missing something here? 👀

Hi . A couple of questions on this - 
1. The document mentions a couple of problems - ingesting OOO samples and ingesting old samples. 
    Is ingesting old samples also implemented as part of this PR ?
2. Is there a flag to enable this feature ?

> The document mentions a couple of problems - ingesting OOO samples and ingesting old samples.
Is ingesting old samples also implemented as part of this PR ?

Yes its implemented, a sample is too old if its older than the window you configure. Else its ingested and its just out of order.

> Is there a flag to enable this feature ?

You can enable it doing this in your config file:
```
storage:
  tsdb:
    out_of_order_time_window: 30m
```
Is there a max value for out_of_order_time_window ?
No, there is no limit. I have only experience running this in production with a max window of 1 month. More should be feasible. No big impact on resources expected.

issue_context.title: Enable handling of overlapping blocks by default
issue_context.body:
Prometheus has had the support for handling overlapping blocks (both during compaction and querying) for a very long time, and it has been used by Thanos, Cortex, Mimir at large scale.

I propose we enable them by default now and not hard fail on finding overlapping blocks. I also propose we still have the switch to disable compaction of overlapping blocks because it is useful and required by downstream consumers with out-of-order feature (what that I mean Mimir, but will also be required by Cortex when they support out-of-order ingestion).

cc @bwplotka
comments: Yes, I like it. It proven to work pretty well for us too.
In which case are overlapping blocks not a bug in regular Prometheus?

> In which case are overlapping blocks not a bug in regular Prometheus?

There can be some unknown races in TSDB that can make blocks overlapping (very rare and idk if we have any, maybe there was a report about some race with compaction). But even in that case, I don't think we should fail hard because some rare race occurred, and gracefully handle it. We log a warning when overlapping blocks are found, so if we come across it, we can see what was the reason then instead of stopping Prometheus from functioning.

Also I think it helps in ease of use when working with out of order and backfilling, you don't have to do an extra step of enabling overlapping blocks (while also having to remember that overlapping blocks need to be enabled).

> We log a warning when overlapping blocks are found, so if we come across it, we can see what was the reason then instead of stopping Prometheus from functioning.

If its that much rare and the codebase can already handle querying from multiple overlapping blocks I think thats another reason to simply enable overlapping blocks by default :+1:

review_comments:
I think I understand what we are trying to do here - to link OOO chunks with normal chunk. However it feels to me like we abuse chunks abstraction. Why can't we store those relations outside of chunk boundary?

It gets really convoluted to think about chunk Meta as `Metadata for a chunk that also can have linked out of order chunks` 🤔

It feels weird there is a different chunk encoding for exactly the same encoding 🤔  This has high risk of making spaghetti code out of very clear chunk abstractions.

I know you do that for ChunkMapper to does not have extra bit:

> We will share the memory mapped files for in-order and out-of-order chunks, hence no additional artifacts here. We will add one bit to the memory mapped chunk metadata to identify the out-of-order chunks.

I wonder if there is a way to do it in more clean way - perhaps:

* Adding that one byte to ChunkMapping
* Making sure ChunkMapping does not need to hold this information? 🤔
TBD in next PRs
Great work on tests!
Why do we need a separate switch?

Imagine you turn on and then off out of order. You local filesystem may still have overlapping blocks because you had out of order on and you want to query them. In that scenario you want to keep `AllowOverlappingQueries` set to true.

For compaction is different. When OOO is true the actual implementation expectes to generate overlapping compacted blocks if ooo samples were received. However if OOO is false we're never expecting overlapping compacted blocks.

This switch was added to also be helpful to downstream users where you want vertical queries but not vertical compaction. With the proposal of always allowing overlapping blocks in Prometheus, we will be able to get rid of the switch for overlapping queries and only have it for compactions later as a follow up work.
Do we need to have this in goroutine? It feels sequential to `d:= range decoded`

It appears to be sequential if you look at the record processing (there too it is sequential for a shard, not totally), but decoding and processing are the 2 parallel things here. So having them in parallel speeds up the replay. We do the same for WAL replay and we had seen nearly 2x improvement that time I think.
If we want different encoding, let's have different encoding. I don't see anything special in this OOO Chunk other than helper for storing temporary `[]sample`
missing commentary on public API
This feels suspicious and prone to errors. Are we sure we never leak goroutines on other types of errors? Also should we use `errors.Is`?
We seem to be doing exactly same for existing WAL replay, so I would tend to believe that it works fine like this.
It's kind of interesting that `WBL` (wrtie behind log) has same implementation as `WAL`... It's a bit of code smell and abusing WAL perhaps. Let's see...

I think we have to refactor this method. It's quite hard to read and review. There are just too many lines and deep indentations to follow. I commented on one content of `if` body where either I have no clue what I am reading or the author of the comment did not have clue 🙈 

We could consider refactoring it in other PRs, since you tested it heavily already (once we clarify comments), but I just wanted to point out that I doubt **I can reliably tell if this `Commit` method makes sense or not** ):

I will add a TODO to simplify it in future. The most complicated part for me personally tends to be `collectOOORecords()` in Commit().

Regarding the comment on the above if block - the comment was a little complex. I will simplify it.
